opus-5.5.text:
I think it's extremely important. In fact, I'd say it's one of the most fundamental questions for embodied intelligence right now.

Look at how autonomous driving developed. Cars are already on the road, and every car can collect data while it drives. Tesla has millions of vehicles feeding back real-world data, so the data flywheel is built into the business. Even so, the autonomous driving industry still relies heavily on simulation. The reason is the long tail. The really dangerous corner cases, like a child running into the street or a strange construction zone, are rare in real data. You can't wait for them to happen thousands of times, so you need simulation to reconstruct, vary, and amplify those scenarios.

Embodied intelligence, especially general-purpose robots that manipulate objects, has it much harder. There's no fleet of millions of humanoid robots already deployed in homes and factories. So the data flywheel hasn't started yet. If you rely only on teleoperation, where a person controls the robot to collect demonstrations, it's very expensive and slow. Maybe you get a few hundred or a few thousand hours. Compare that to large language models, which train on essentially the whole internet. The gap is several orders of magnitude.

So my view is that for embodied intelligence, simulation and synthetic data aren't just a supplement. They may be the main way to bootstrap the first generation of truly generalizable models. In simulation you can generate huge numbers of objects, scenes, lighting conditions, and physical properties. You can randomize everything and produce billions of frames of grasping or manipulation data at a cost far below real-world collection. Then you use a smaller amount of real data to close the sim-to-real gap and align the model with reality.

Of course, building a good simulation data pipeline is very hard. You need realistic assets, accurate physics, especially for contact and deformable objects, and good rendering so the visual gap isn't too large. You also need automated ways to generate successful trajectories, so you're not relying on humans for each one. That's an engineering system, not just an algorithm. Whoever builds that pipeline well gets a real advantage, because data is the bottleneck.

So I'd sum it up this way: for autonomous driving, simulation is the key to solving the long tail. For embodied intelligence, simulation may be the key to getting started at all.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses simulation’s value and engineering challenges, but does not report that proofs of concept at small and midsize autonomous-driving companies fail to reach production.

r002.rationale: The candidate says a well-built simulation pipeline gives companies a real advantage and may be key to getting embodied intelligence started, conveying that companies without one risk a competitive disadvantage.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is one of the most underestimated pieces of the whole stack, and I'd actually frame it less as a "pipeline" and more as the core capability that decides whether you have a real system or a demo.

Start with the fundamental problem. For autonomous driving, and even more so for embodied intelligence, the thing you want to learn is a policy, which means the data you need is not static images or text. It's closed-loop interaction. The model takes an action, the world responds, and the next observation depends on what the model did. You cannot collect that passively from the internet, and you cannot collect enough of it from real vehicles or real robots at the pace the models now demand. Real-world data is expensive, slow, dangerous in exactly the cases you care most about, and distributed in a way that is almost the opposite of what you need. You end up with millions of frames of a car driving straight on a highway and almost nothing on the long tail where the system actually fails.

Simulation is the only lever that changes that economics. But I want to be precise about what "building the pipeline" means, because people often reduce it to "we bought a rendering engine." The hard part is not rendering. The hard part is three things.

First, scenario generation. Can you systematically produce the situations that matter, including ones no one has seen yet? That's a data problem and increasingly a generative-model problem, not a graphics problem.

Second, fidelity where it counts. For driving that means sensor behavior and traffic agent behavior. For embodied intelligence it means contact, friction, deformable objects, the physics that actually determines whether a grasp succeeds. A beautiful scene with wrong contact dynamics is worse than useless, because the policy learns confident wrong behavior.

Third, and this is where most teams underinvest, the loop back. Simulation has to be connected to evaluation and to the failures you observe in the real world. The value compounds only when a real failure becomes a sim scenario within days, you generate thousands of variations, you retrain, and you verify in the same sim before you touch hardware. If sim is a separate team producing a dataset once a quarter, you've captured maybe ten percent of its value.

On the sim-to-real gap, my view has shifted. Five years ago the gap was the reason people were skeptical. Now I think of it as a quantity you actively manage rather than an obstacle you hope disappears. Domain randomization, real-to-sim reconstruction, and learned world models all narrow it from different directions, and the models themselves have become far more tolerant of imperfect data as long as the diversity is there. The remaining gap you handle with a relatively small amount of real data for alignment, which is a much better deal than trying to do everything in the real world.

The embodied case is honestly where I think this becomes decisive. In driving you at least have a fleet and a fairly constrained action space. In robotics you have no fleet, enormous action spaces, and tasks that vary across every kitchen and every warehouse. Whoever builds the data flywheel there, with simulation as the engine and real deployment as the correction signal, is going to pull far ahead. So if you ask me where I'd put engineering effort in these organizations, the simulation and data infrastructure would be near the very top, right alongside the model work itself. It's not supporting infrastructure. It's the product.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a real system with a demo in general, but does not report hearing that simulation proofs of concept at small and midsize autonomous-driving companies fail to reach production.

r002.rationale: The response says embodied-intelligence companies that build the simulation-driven data flywheel will pull far ahead, clearly implying that those without such pipelines risk a lasting competitive disadvantage.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re fundamental, because both autonomous driving and embodied intelligence need to learn from interactions with the physical world, and collecting those interactions in reality is expensive and slow. Some situations are also dangerous or difficult to reproduce. Simulation gives us a way to generate those situations repeatedly and at scale.

But the key is the word “pipeline.” It’s not enough to build a simulator that looks realistic. You need a process for deciding which scenarios to generate, producing useful data, training models, and then checking whether those models actually perform better in the real world. The results of that testing should guide the next round of simulation.

For autonomous driving, that might mean exploring unusual traffic interactions or challenging conditions. For embodied intelligence, you also have to capture how actions change the environment—contact, friction, objects moving, and so on. Visual realism alone won’t tell you whether a robot can successfully grasp an object.

So I see simulation and real-world data as complementary. Real-world experience helps us identify where simulation is wrong, while simulation lets us explore variations that would be costly to collect physically. The most important measure is whether that cycle improves real-world capability and reliability, rather than simply how much synthetic data we can produce.

r002.rationale: It calls simulation pipelines fundamental and explains their benefits, but does not say that companies that forgo them may face a long-term competitive weakness.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re foundational. For both autonomous driving and embodied intelligence, the challenge is not simply collecting more data; it’s getting the right coverage of situations and knowing what the data actually tests.

In autonomous driving, you need to study rare, safety-critical events that are difficult to collect repeatedly in the real world. Simulation lets you vary conditions systematically and examine how a system responds. For embodied intelligence, interaction adds another layer: an action changes the environment, and the next observation depends on that action. You need a pipeline that captures this loop, including the relevant physics.

But generating a large volume of simulated data is not enough. The important question is whether it improves performance in the real world. That means building a feedback loop: identify failures in real environments, reproduce and vary them in simulation, train or evaluate the model, and then validate again in reality.

So I would treat the simulation data pipeline as a core research capability. Its value comes from making experimentation faster, more controlled, and more informative—not just from producing more samples.
